title: Scientists Report Blood Traces in a 115-Million-Year-Old Dinosaur Bone
paragraphs: Researchers led by Curtin University in Australia say they have found chemical traces of blood in a dinosaur bone that is about 115 million years old. The bone comes from Aratasaurus museunacionali, a meat-eating dinosaur that lived in what is now northeastern Brazil. The results were published in the journal PNAS.

Inside narrow channels in the leg bones, the team saw many mineralised red blood cells. Chemical tests also found heme, a part of hemoglobin, which carries oxygen in blood, and amino acids linked to collagen. The cells were covered by a mineral called hausmannite, which may have helped protect them over time.

The scientists believe the animal was buried quickly in low-oxygen mud full of microbes, but this is an explanation, not a proven fact. The study looked at only one dinosaur, and the idea that such molecules can last so long has been debated for years, so other teams will want to check the results. Professor Kliti Grice's research was supported by an Australian Research Council fellowship.

questions.q: What did chemical tests find in the bone?
questions.a: Heme, a part of hemoglobin, and amino acids linked to collagen.

questions.q: Why should other teams check the results?
questions.a: The study covers only one dinosaur and the idea has been debated for years.
